name: Blackout curtains
lead: Blackout curtains are window coverings made from, or lined with, an opaque fabric that blocks most outside light from entering a room. The term blackout refers to a foam-backed opaque fabric most often seen as hotel curtain lining or drapery [1]. They are popular with people who sleep during the day, with parents of infants, and with residents of areas with heavy night-time light pollution [1].

In looksmaxxing and sleep-optimisation circles they are treated as a basic bedroom measure for darker, more consistent sleep. The chain people describe runs from a darker room to more uninterrupted sleep to better-rested skin, eyes and mood the next day; Wikipedia's article on sleep deprivation lists under-eye puffiness among the visible effects of too little sleep.[11] Beyond light control, blackout fabrics are also said to provide some thermal insulation and noise dampening because of their density.[1]

Evidence specific to curtains comes from surveys and observational studies. Surveys show they are among the most common light-reduction measures adults adopt,[7] observational studies link outdoor artificial light at night with metabolic disease,[4] and sleep-hygiene guidance recommends a very dark bedroom.[8] A representative Norwegian survey found no association between blackout-curtain use and chronic insomnia disorder,[6] and no published trial tests curtains directly against an uncovered window.
infobox: Ordinary household textile; not a medical device

paras: Blackout fabric is made by coating a base textile with layers of foam, each layer being called a pass. In a 2-pass blackout, a black foam layer is applied first and a white or light-coloured layer is applied over it. In a 3-pass blackout, a white layer goes on first, then black foam, then a final white or light layer [1]. The process is credited to Baltimore-based Rockland Industries [1].

Because the black foam layer shows through the fabric side of a 2-pass material, a 2-pass blackout is not generally used as a decorative fabric by itself. A 3-pass material can serve as decorative fabric and blackout lining in a single piece [1]. Blackout is also used for wallpaper, projector screens and planetarium domes [1].

Curtains in general come in many heading styles, lengths and fabrics, and the Grokipedia entry on curtains lists blackout curtains among the common types alongside sheer, pleated, grommet-top and café styles [2]. Edge gaps around a curtain can still let light in, so fit, overlap and rod placement affect how dark the room becomes.

Curtains as a category are old, with the Grokipedia curtains article tracing hangings of linen and other materials to ancient Egypt and later to European castles and Renaissance interiors [2]. That article is AI-generated and its history is not independently verified here. The foam-coated blackout process is a modern industrial development attributed to Rockland Industries [1].

Sleep-hygiene advice itself has a history: Paolo Mantegazza wrote on related ideas in 1864, Willard Moyer coined 'hygiene of sleep' in 1903, and Peter Hauri's 1977 book brought a list of behavioural rules into sleep medicine.[8]

Light reaching the eyes during sleep can arouse the sleeper. Light at night can suppress melatonin, the hormone that signals night to the body; blue light in roughly the 460 to 480 nm range suppresses it most, and suppression grows with brightness and duration.[9] Wikipedia's article on melatonin says light before and during sleep may impair sleep quality through this route.[9] The light pollution article notes that strong outdoor light entering a home through a window can cause sleep deprivation and that some US cities have adopted lighting standards against such light trespass.[10]

A blackout curtain aims to lower the amount of street, vehicle or early-morning light entering the room. Wikipedia notes use by shift workers sleeping in daylight and in nurseries where darkness is said to help babies sleep.[1] Sleep-hygiene guidance recommends a quiet, very dark and cool bedroom, and notes that shift workers can also reduce disruptions by silencing phones and posting signs on doors.[8]
No randomized trial of blackout curtains for sleep or appearance outcomes exists. The available human data are surveys and observational studies.

A 2017 population-based Norwegian telephone survey of 1,001 adults described age and sex differences in bedroom habits and preferences, including whether bedroom windows were left open [5]. A follow-up analysis of the same sample compared people with chronic insomnia disorder with good sleepers. Insomnia was associated with worse bed comfort, more noise, and higher summer bedroom temperature, but the authors found no association with the use of blackout curtains, among other characteristics [6]. The design is cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether curtains change sleep.

A 2025 nationwide cross-sectional survey of 5,006 Polish adults aged 18 to 64 found blackout curtains to be the most common individual measure for reducing night-time light, used by 41.4 percent of respondents, ahead of limiting evening screen time (17.6 percent); eye masks were the least common at 3.9 percent, and 65 percent had adopted at least one such measure [7].

A hospital-admissions study in Ningxia, China, estimated that about 26.8 percent of metabolic-disease cases were attributable to outdoor artificial light at night, with men aged 46 to 59 appearing more susceptible; the authors proposed measures such as universal access to indoor blackout curtains [4]. This is an ecological estimate of outdoor light exposure and does not test curtains.

A survey of nurses on shift work listed blackout curtains among interventions respondents were interested in, alongside an on-site exercise facility, nutrition consulting and block scheduling [3]. It measured interest rather than outcomes.

Blackout curtains are ordinary household textiles and no specific adverse effects are documented. Practical considerations noted in consumer guidance include light leaking around the edges and reduced morning daylight, which some people find makes waking harder. Some users pair curtains with a sunrise alarm or open them on waking; these are practices rather than studied recommendations.

In sleep-focused looksmaxxing, darkness is often presented as the first step toward deeper sleep, on the theory that sleep quality influences skin condition, under-eye appearance and hormones. Curtains are commonly grouped with sleep masks, white noise machines, cooler bedroom temperatures and consistent wake times, in line with general sleep-hygiene guidance.[8] The sleep-deprivation literature summarised on Wikipedia lists eye bags among visible effects, and one study cited there found extreme sleepiness made people feel about ten years older.[11] No study has tested curtains against appearance outcomes.

On T Nation, members mention blackout curtains in sleep threads: one poster describes deeper darkness at night and less sun in the eyes during daytime sleep, and another lists complete darkness among bedroom improvements for broken sleep while training.[12][13]

Product descriptions typically distinguish between 2-pass and 3-pass construction, full blackout versus partial room-darkening fabric, thermal lining, and heading types that affect how closely the panel seals against the wall [1]. Prices commonly fall between about $25 and $80 per panel set. Manufacturers' light-blocking percentages are retailer claims rather than independent measurements.

timeline.event: Paolo Mantegazza's book contains early ideas later grouped under sleep hygiene.[8]
Willard Moyer coins the phrase 'hygiene of sleep'.[8]
Peter Hauri's book brings behavioural sleep rules into modern sleep medicine.[8]
WHO's cancer agency classifies shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable carcinogen.[10]
Norwegian population survey describes bedroom habits and preferences in 1,001 adults.[5]
Follow-up analysis finds no association between blackout-curtain use and chronic insomnia disorder.[6]
Polish survey of 5,006 adults finds blackout curtains the most common night-light measure (41.4%).[7]

lore.intro: On T Nation and in sleep-optimisation circles, blackout curtains are one of the first bedroom changes people mention for better sleep.[12][13]

claims.believers: A T Nation poster reports that deep darkness 'seems to help some' and that curtains stop sunlight waking them during daytime sleep.[12]
claims.experts: Sleep-hygiene guidance recommends a very dark bedroom, and melatonin research describes light before and during sleep as capable of impairing sleep; no trial has tested curtains specifically.[8][9]

claims.believers: Members include complete darkness in lists of bedroom changes for broken sleep.[13]
claims.experts: A representative Norwegian survey found no association between blackout-curtain use and chronic insomnia disorder, though the design cannot show cause.[6]

claims.claim: Better sleep from a dark room improves how you look.
claims.believers: Sleep-focused looksmaxxers connect rest to skin, under-eye appearance and energy.
claims.experts: Reference works list under-eye puffiness among effects of sleep deprivation; no study links curtains to appearance outcomes.[11]

claims.believers: Authors of a Chinese hospital-admissions study suggested universal access to indoor blackout curtains.[4]
claims.experts: The study estimated outdoor light attributable cases ecologically and did not test curtains.[4]

angle.text: People hang blackout curtains to make the bedroom dark enough to sleep through early light, with the aim of waking rested. Looksmaxxers link sleep to skin, under-eye appearance, mood and training recovery.
